title: Why Diesel Costs More Than Gasoline — and When the Flip Happened
excerpt: National diesel is averaging $6.38 a gallon, nearly $2 above gasoline. Three structural reasons — demand, cleaner-fuel rules and taxes — plus the Iran war's supply shock explain the gap.
body:
• Diesel averaged $6.38 a gallon nationally this week, up from about $3.60 a year ago, according to NPR's The Indicator newsletter. On September 21, AAA recorded an all-time high of $6.51.
  • Diesel has cost more than regular gasoline since September 2004. The U.S. Energy Information Administration points to three structural reasons: surging global demand, costlier ultra-low-sulfur refining rules, and higher federal taxes — 24.4 cents per gallon for diesel versus 18.4 cents for gasoline.
  • The current spike is supply-driven: the Iran and Ukraine wars have limited refining capacity and crude production, with the Strait of Hormuz closure tightening the market. Some Republican lawmakers are lobbying President Trump to ban diesel exports; the American Petroleum Institute opposes the idea.
  • What it means for you: diesel now costs roughly $2 a gallon more than regular gasoline. Diesel powers trucking, trains, farm equipment and heating, so sustained highs can push up prices on everything shipped — and the Fed's interest-rate hikes cannot fix supply-driven fuel inflation.

The next time you drive past a gas station, look at the diesel number. This week it averaged $6.38 a gallon nationally — nearly double the $3.60 average a year ago, according to NPR's The Indicator newsletter. Two weeks earlier, AAA logged an all-time record of $6.51.

It was not always this way. Diesel used to cost less than regular gasoline. The flip happened in September 2004, and with few exceptions diesel has stayed pricier ever since. The reasons are structural — and the current record is a separate, sharper story about war and refining.

Context and Background

The U.S. Energy Information Administration attributes the 2004 flip to three forces. First, demand: in the early 2000s, China and India were motorizing and industrializing, says Clay Seigl, who leads the energy practice at Beacon Global Strategies — agriculture, construction and infrastructure projects, all diesel-powered. In Europe, diesel grew from 13.8 percent of new car registrations in 1990 to 53 percent in 2007.

Second, air quality: in June 2006, federal rules cut the allowable sulfur in diesel fuel, and producing ultra-low-sulfur diesel costs more in refining and distribution. Third, taxes: a 1993 increase set the federal excise tax at 24.4 cents per gallon for on-highway diesel, six cents above gasoline's 18.4 cents. State taxes vary, but diesel is taxed at a slightly higher level across the nation overall.

One more structural pressure: diesel and jet fuel are both middle distillates from the same refining stream. When jet fuel prices climb, refiners tilt production toward jet fuel and diesel supply tightens — which is exactly the kind of squeeze now hitting holiday travelers booking Thanksgiving flights.

Impact and Analysis

The current record is different from the long-term trend. This one is supply. The Iran and Ukraine wars have limited refining capacity and crude production, while diesel demand from trucks, trains, generator farms and heating stays essential. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz and other oil routes has tightened the market further.

The politics have turned loud. Republican members of Congress have been lobbying President Trump to ban diesel exports; the administration is weighing the move, and the American Petroleum Institute is firmly against it. Regional extremes are already stark: diesel hit a record $7.81 a gallon in Kern County, California, while regular gas topped $5.85 there, according to a Yahoo report.

"Diesel is literally the fuel the U.S. economy runs on. It's more fuel efficient than gas. And when you're hauling tons of furniture or wheat or candles or whatever goods you want across the country, diesel is generally how you do it."

— Stephan Bisaha, NPR

Higher diesel costs feed inflation in a way the Federal Reserve cannot easily counter. The Fed recently raised interest rates, but as Bisaha told NPR's Steve Inskeep, expensive borrowing does not get more oil out of the Middle East or make it cheaper to refine. So far, trucking companies have not yet fully passed the costs to store shelves — but analysts are bracing for it.

Diaspora Angle

The explanation itself carries the India thread: when the EIA points to surging demand in the early 2000s, India's motorizing boom is part of that demand story. Today, the pain lands on American consumers broadly — including the Indian-American families in trucking and logistics for whom diesel at $6.38 a gallon is the cost line on every mile.

What's Next

Watch the White House on the export-ban question: restricting exports could lower domestic diesel prices but invites industry pushback and trade friction. Watch the Strait of Hormuz and refinery restarts for supply relief. And keep an eye on jet fuel — it competes with diesel for the same refining output, so its climb will shape both Thanksgiving airfares and the diesel price at the pump.
